definition: A running program as the operating system manages it: its own private memory (address space), open files and one or more threads. Threads inside one process share its memory; separate processes share nothing unless they set it up explicitly.
example: A web browser often runs each tab as a separate process, so one crashing tab does not take down the others.

definition: The software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs: it schedules threads onto CPU cores, gives each process its memory and provides system calls for files, networking and synchronisation. Its privileged core is the kernel.
example: Linux, Windows and macOS are operating systems.

definition: The part of the kernel that decides which runnable thread runs on each CPU core next, and for how long. Its choices depend on timing, interrupts and load, so two threads can be interleaved differently on every run.
One particular order in which the individual steps of several concurrent threads end up mixed together. A race condition is a bug that appears in some interleavings and not others.
example: Thread A loads, thread B loads, A stores, B stores: that interleaving of two increments loses an update.

definition: Giving different results on different runs with the same input, because something outside the program's control, such as thread timing, changes. Concurrency bugs are hard to reproduce for this reason.
A bug where two threads (or transactions) both read the same old value, both compute a new value from it, and the second write overwrites the first, so one change vanishes.
example: Both threads read 5 and both store 6: two increments ran, but the counter only rose by one.

definition: A tiny, very fast storage slot inside a processor core that instructions compute on, such as x86's eax. Each thread has its own copy of the registers (saved and restored on a context switch), so a value loaded into a register is private until it is stored back to memory.
An independent processing unit inside a CPU chip that runs its own stream of instructions. A multicore machine runs several threads truly at the same time, one per core.
example: A laptop with 8 cores can run 8 threads in parallel.

definition: An operation that reads a memory location, computes a new value from it and writes it back, such as counter++. Unless it is done as one atomic operation, another thread can run between the read and the write.

An operation that happens as one indivisible step: no other thread can see it half done or slip in between its parts. CPUs provide atomic instructions (such as x86's lock xadd), and C11 and C++11 expose them as atomic types and functions.
example: atomic_fetch_add(&hits, 1) from eight threads never loses an increment.

definition: The property of being atomic: a group of steps either happens entirely, with no other thread observing it midway, or not at all. Atomicity is a separate question from memory ordering, which is about when other memory operations become visible.

An x86 instruction prefix that makes the following read-modify-write instruction (such as add, inc, xadd or cmpxchg) atomic across all cores, by holding the cache line exclusively for the whole operation.
example: lock xadd is the atomic version of xadd.

definition: The x86 instruction that adds 1 to a register or memory location. On memory it is still a read-modify-write that other cores can interleave with, unless it carries the lock prefix.

The family of processor instruction sets from Intel and AMD used by most PCs and servers; x86-64 is its 64-bit form. Its memory model (TSO) is relatively strong: the only reordering it allows is a later load overtaking an earlier store.

A family of processor architectures used in almost all phones and, increasingly, servers and laptops. ARMv8 is weakly ordered: it may reorder most memory accesses unless code uses barriers or acquire/release instructions. ARMv8.1 added single-instruction atomics such as cas and ldadd.
The 2011 edition of the C language standard (ISO/IEC 9899:2011). It added threads, the stdatomic.h atomic types and a formal memory model with data races, happens-before and memory orders.
C++ is a systems programming language derived from C; C++11 is its 2011 standard, which introduced std::thread, std::atomic and the same memory model as C11. Later C++ standards build on it.

The POSIX standard C interface for threads on Unix-like systems such as Linux and macOS: pthread_create starts a thread, pthread_join waits for it to finish, and pthread mutexes and condition variables coordinate them.

The IEEE family of standards (IEEE 1003, also ISO/IEC 9945) defining a common Unix-like operating-system interface: system calls, threads, semaphores and shell utilities. Linux and macOS largely follow it, which is why pthread code ports between them.

In C and C++, a program action for which the standard imposes no requirements at all, such as a data race or reading freed memory. The compiler may assume it never happens, so the result can be anything: wrong answers, crashes or code that seems to work until the next compiler upgrade.

CPython's global interpreter lock: one lock a thread must hold to run Python bytecode, so in a standard build only one thread executes Python code at a time. It keeps the interpreter simple but stops CPU-bound Python threads running in parallel, and it is not a promise that multi-step operations such as += are atomic.
The reference implementation of Python, written in C: the interpreter you get from python.org. Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build without the GIL.
A popular high-level programming language, run here by the CPython interpreter. Its threading module provides threads, locks, semaphores and condition variables.

A CPython build without the global interpreter lock, introduced experimentally in Python 3.13 under PEP 703, so Python threads can run truly in parallel. It relies on finer-grained internal locking instead.
A Python Enhancement Proposal: the design document through which changes to Python are proposed and decided. PEP 703 made the global interpreter lock optional.

The ordering relation a memory model uses to decide which writes a read may see. A happens-before B if A comes first in the same thread (sequenced-before), synchronises-with B across threads (unlock then lock, release then acquire), or is linked to B by a chain of these. Conflicting non-atomic accesses not ordered by it form a data race.
example: The producer's write of data happens-before the consumer's read when a release store and an acquire load link them.

definition: Two memory accesses to the same location where at least one is a write. Conflicting accesses from different threads must be ordered by synchronisation, or both be atomic, to avoid a data race.

A race where a thread checks a condition and then acts on it as a separate step, so the condition can change in between, even if each step takes a lock internally. The fix is to make check and action one atomic unit.
example: Two threads both see a balance of 150, both pass "balance >= 100" and both withdraw 100, leaving -50.

aliases: time of check to time of use
definition: Time-of-check to time-of-use: the check-then-act race, especially the security bug where a program checks a file (its permissions or existence) and later uses it, after an attacker has swapped it, for example for a symbolic link.

A special file that just contains a path to another file or directory; opening it opens the target. Attackers use symbolic links in TOCTOU attacks by swapping a checked file for a link to a sensitive one.

Describes code or an object that behaves correctly when called from several threads at once, usually by locking or using atomics internally. Thread-safe pieces do not make a sequence of calls safe: that needs its own atomic unit.
A piece of code that accesses shared state and must never be run by more than one thread at a time. A lock is taken on entry and released on exit; keeping critical sections short limits contention.

The textbook parts of a thread's loop around a critical section: the entry section asks permission to enter (for example, takes a lock), the exit section gives it back, and the remainder section is everything else the thread does.

The guarantee that at most one thread is inside a critical section at any time. It is the first requirement of any critical-section solution and the job of a lock; "mutex" is short for mutual exclusion.
The critical-section requirement that, once a thread has asked to enter, only a limited number of other entries can happen ahead of it. It rules out starvation.
example: Strict alternation bounds waiting at one: the other thread can enter at most once ahead of you.

definition: When several threads want the same lock (or cache line) at the same moment, so some must wait. "Uncontended" means nobody else wants it at that moment; good lock designs make that case very cheap and pay extra only under contention.

Gary Peterson's 1981 mutual-exclusion algorithm for two threads using only loads and stores of two flags and a turn variable. It is correct under sequential consistency but fails on real hardware with store buffers unless it uses sequentially consistent atomics.

A naive two-thread lock where a shared turn variable forces the threads to take turns. It gives mutual exclusion but violates progress: a thread can be kept out of an empty critical section just because it is the other thread's turn.

Leslie Lamport's 1979 memory model: every run behaves as if all threads' operations happened in one single interleaved order that respects each thread's program order. Real CPUs and compilers do not give it to ordinary accesses; in C11 you get it from atomics with the default memory_order_seq_cst.
The order in which one thread's operations appear in its source code. Compilers and CPUs may execute them in a different order as long as that thread alone cannot tell; other threads can.

A small queue inside each CPU core where writes wait before reaching the cache, so the core need not stall on every store. A later load can complete while an earlier store is still buffered, which is how a load overtakes a store on x86. The store-buffering litmus test shows the effect.

Creating an object only when it is first needed rather than at start-up. With threads it becomes a race: two threads can both see "not created yet" and both build it, or one can see a half-built object.
A shared counter kept only for reporting, such as bytes sent. Its increments must be atomic so none are lost, but nothing else depends on its ordering, so relaxed atomics are enough.
C++'s standard growable array. It is not safe for concurrent modification: two threads appending at once can corrupt its internal pointers, not just lose a value.
Java's standard hash table class (java.util.HashMap). It is not synchronised, and concurrent modification can corrupt it, which is why java.util.concurrent offers ConcurrentHashMap.

A database setting that controls how much concurrent transactions see of each other's changes, from read uncommitted up to serializable. Stronger levels prevent anomalies such as lost updates, at some cost in concurrency.

A data-race detector built into the Clang and GCC compilers, enabled with -fsanitize=thread. It instruments memory accesses and reports conflicting accesses not ordered by happens-before, but only on code paths the run actually executes.
The GNU Compiler Collection: the standard open-source C and C++ compiler on most Linux systems.
The C, C++ and Objective-C compiler of the LLVM project, and the default compiler on macOS.
A Valgrind tool that detects data races, lock-ordering problems and misuse of the POSIX threads API in C and C++ programs.
An instrumentation framework that runs a program on a simulated CPU to check it as it runs. It is best known for finding memory errors; Helgrind and DRD are its thread-error detectors.
The OS stopping a running thread without its cooperation, typically on a timer interrupt at the end of its time slice, to run another. A preempted lock holder keeps the lock while it is not running.
A machine with only one CPU core, so only one thread runs at a time; concurrency there comes only from interrupts and preemption.
A signal from hardware (a timer, a disk, a network card) that makes a CPU core pause what it is doing and run an interrupt handler. The timer interrupt is what lets the scheduler preempt threads.
The kernel code that runs in response to an interrupt. It runs in a context that must never sleep, so it can use spinlocks but not sleeping mutexes.
Interrupt request: a hardware interrupt signal, or the line or number that identifies it.

An interrupt that the CPU can be told to ignore for a while ("mask"), for example with x86's cli instruction. Kernels mask interrupts briefly to protect short sections from interrupt handlers on the same core.
An interrupt that cannot be blocked by disabling interrupts, reserved for urgent events such as hardware errors and watchdog timers. Disabling interrupts therefore does not exclude it.

Total store order: x86's memory model. Each core's stores become visible in program order, and the only visible reordering is a later load completing before an earlier store to a different address leaves the store buffer.

The fixed-size block in which data moves between memory and CPU caches: 64 bytes on most x86 chips and many ARM chips. Cores manage ownership line by line, so threads writing anything in the same line fight over it.

A C and C++ type qualifier telling the compiler that every access must really happen, intended for memory-mapped hardware. It gives no atomicity and no ordering between threads in C or C++. Java's volatile is different: it does give acquire/release ordering.

A compiler setting, such as -O0 (no optimisation) or -O2 (most optimisations), that controls how aggressively code is transformed. Higher levels reorder, merge and remove memory accesses more freely, which often exposes data races.
x86's atomic fetch-and-add instruction: it adds a value to memory and returns the old value as one indivisible step across all cores. atomic_fetch_add usually compiles to it.
The C11 function that atomically adds to an atomic integer and returns its previous value; atomic_fetch_sub subtracts. The _explicit forms take a memory order.
An atomic instruction that adds to a memory location and returns its old value, used for counters and ticket locks. On x86 it is lock xadd.
C's basic signed integer type, 32 bits wide (−2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647) on current mainstream platforms. A plain int has no atomicity between threads; atomic_int does.
The true/false type in C (via stdbool.h, and a keyword since C23) and in C++. A plain bool flag shared between threads without atomics is a data race.

A C11 type (or C++ std::atomic) whose loads, stores and read-modify-writes are atomic and take part in the memory model, so concurrent access is not a data race. atomic_int, atomic_bool and atomic_long are shorthands for _Atomic int, _Atomic bool and _Atomic long.

C11 functions that read (atomic_load) or write (atomic_store) an atomic object, or replace the value and return the old one (atomic_exchange). Without _explicit they use seq_cst ordering; the _explicit forms take a memory order.
C11's simplest atomic type: a flag that can only be set with test-and-set or cleared. It is the one atomic type guaranteed to be lock-free, which makes it a natural spinlock.
Real elapsed time, as a clock on the wall would measure it. The memory model has no notion of it: an access happening "a second later" gets no ordering guarantee from that alone.

A synchronisation object that only one thread at a time can hold (or, for a read-write lock, one writer or many readers). Threads take it before a critical section and release it afterwards; mutexes and spinlocks are kinds of lock.
The POSIX threads mutex type. pthread_mutex_lock takes it (sleeping if another thread holds it) and pthread_mutex_unlock releases it; on Linux glibc builds it on futexes.
A CPU instruction that only runs in kernel mode, such as disabling interrupts. A user program that tries one gets a fault instead.
The privileged CPU mode in which the operating-system kernel runs and can execute privileged instructions. Entering it for a system call and returning costs far more than an ordinary function call.
The unprivileged side of the system where ordinary programs run, as opposed to the kernel. Code there cannot put a thread to sleep or touch hardware directly; it must make a system call.
A computer with more than one CPU core or processor sharing memory, so threads can run truly at the same time.
Symmetric multiprocessing: several identical cores sharing one memory and one kernel, any of which can run any thread. Linux first supported it in version 2.0 (1996).
An atomic instruction that writes 1 to a memory location and returns its old value in one step. If the old value was 0, the caller has just taken the lock. On x86 it is xchg.
x86's exchange instruction: it swaps a register with memory, and is automatically locked (atomic) when one operand is memory. It serves as test-and-set and also acts as a full barrier.

An atomic instruction that sets a memory location to a new value only if it still holds an expected value, and reports whether it did. It is the building block of lock-free algorithms. C11 calls it atomic_compare_exchange and, on failure, writes the value it actually found back into expected.
example: CAS(&l, 0, 1) takes a free lock: it succeeds only if l was still 0.

definition: x86's compare-and-exchange instruction. With the lock prefix it is an atomic compare-and-swap of up to 8 bytes.
An x86-64 instruction that compares and swaps 16 bytes at once (atomically with the lock prefix): enough for a pointer plus a 64-bit counter, as tagged pointers need.

A pair of instructions used on ARM, POWER and RISC-V. Load-linked reads a location and starts watching it; store-conditional writes only if nobody has written the location since, and otherwise fails so the code retries. ARM's versions are ldxr and stxr.

A compare-and-swap that reports failure even though the value matched. C11's weak form (compare_exchange_weak) is allowed to do this, because LL/SC can lose its reservation for unrelated reasons; it is harmless inside a retry loop.
ARMv8.1 single-instruction atomics: ldadd is an atomic fetch-and-add and swp an atomic exchange (cas, also added in ARMv8.1, is compare-and-swap). ARMv8.0 has to build these from ldxr/stxr loops.

A lock whose waiters loop ("spin"), repeatedly checking it, instead of sleeping. It is fast when the holder releases within a very short time on another core and wasteful when the holder is preempted.

A fair spinlock built from two counters: each arriving thread takes the next ticket with fetch-and-add and waits until the now-serving counter reaches its number, so threads enter in arrival (FIFO) order.

When a fixed-width counter passes its maximum and starts again from 0: a 16-bit counter goes from 65,535 to 0. Algorithms that use counters or tags must make sure a wrapped value cannot be mistaken for an old one.
Linux's default spinlock implementation, based on the MCS lock: waiters queue up and each spins on its own queue entry instead of the shared lock word, which cuts cache-line traffic.

The hardware protocol (such as MESI) that keeps every core's cached copy of a memory location consistent. Before writing a cache line, a core must take exclusive ownership of it, invalidating other cores' copies; that transfer is what makes contended locks slow.

When several cores write the same cache line in turn, so exclusive ownership moves back and forth between their caches. Each move is much slower than a cached access, so a contended lock word slows down even its holder.

A spinlock refinement that spins on a plain atomic read, which all waiters can share in their caches, and attempts the expensive test-and-set only when the lock looks free. This greatly reduces cache-line traffic.
Waiting for a while before retrying after failing to get a lock, often doubling the delay each time (exponential backoff), to reduce contention.
The longest stretch of CPU time the scheduler gives a thread before it may preempt it to run another, typically a few milliseconds.
example: A 10 ms time slice means a spinning waiter can waste 10 ms each time it is scheduled.

definition: The Linux kernel's real-time configuration, merged into the mainline kernel in version 6.12 (2024). It makes most kernel code preemptible and turns ordinary spinlock_t locks into sleeping locks, so high-priority tasks get predictable latency.
The Linux kernel's standard spinlock type. On ordinary kernels it disables preemption while held; under PREEMPT_RT it becomes a sleeping lock. raw_spinlock_t always really spins.

A Linux kernel call that saves the current interrupt state, disables interrupts on the local CPU and takes a spinlock; spin_unlock_irqrestore undoes it. It is used when the same lock may also be taken in an interrupt handler.
A lock whose waiters are put to sleep by the kernel and woken when it is released, instead of spinning. It costs a system call when contended but wastes no CPU while waiting.

Linux's "fast userspace mutex": a 32-bit integer in user memory plus the futex() system call. Locking and unlocking use atomic instructions on the integer in user space; the kernel is called only to sleep (FUTEX_WAIT) or wake (FUTEX_WAKE) when threads actually collide.

The futex operation "put me to sleep on this address, but only if it still holds the expected value". The kernel checks the value and queues the thread atomically with respect to wakers, so a wakeup cannot be lost; if the value differs it returns EAGAIN at once.
The futex operation that wakes up to a given number of threads sleeping on an address. An unlock calls it only when the lock word shows there may be waiters.

A bug where a thread checks a condition and decides to sleep, but the wakeup arrives between the check and the sleep, so it sleeps forever. It is prevented by making check-and-sleep atomic, as FUTEX_WAIT and condition-variable wait do.
Former maintainer of glibc and author of the paper "Futexes Are Tricky", which explains how to build a correct mutex on futexes, and of "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory".

The common, cheap route through code, such as taking an uncontended lock with one atomic instruction in user space. The slow path handles the rarer, expensive case, here sleeping and waking through the kernel.
The GNU C Library, the standard C library on most Linux distributions. It implements pthread mutexes, condition variables and read-write locks on top of futexes.
Windows' slim reader/writer lock: a pointer-sized lock with a user-space fast path that only calls into the kernel when it must wait.
A Windows function (Windows 8 and later) that sleeps until the value at a memory address changes: the Windows counterpart of FUTEX_WAIT.
Apple's low-level lock for macOS and iOS. Waiters sleep in the kernel rather than spin, and, as the name says, it makes no promise about the order in which waiters get the lock.
Microsoft's operating system for PCs and servers.
Apple's operating system for Mac computers, a Unix-like system that largely follows POSIX.
The open-source Unix-like operating-system kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991. It runs most servers, Android phones and many embedded devices.

A mutex that, on contention, first spins briefly (betting that the holder is running on another core and will release soon) and only then sleeps. The Linux kernel's mutex does this "optimistic spinning" while the owner is running.
The idea that a lock belongs to the thread that took it, and only that thread may release it. Ownership enables error checking, re-entrancy and priority inheritance; semaphores have no owner.

Python's basic lock. It is not re-entrant and has no owner, so any thread may release it, and a thread that acquires it twice blocks itself forever. Use it with "with lock:" so it is released even on an exception.
Python's re-entrant lock: it records the owning thread and a count, so the owner can acquire it again and must release it the same number of times.

A lock that the thread already holding it can acquire again without blocking itself. It keeps an owner and a count and is fully released only when the count returns to zero. Also called a recursive mutex.
A pthread mutex type that reports misuse with an error code, such as EPERM for unlocking a mutex the caller does not own, instead of undefined behaviour.
A pthread mutex that, if its owner dies while holding it, lets the next locker take it with the error EOWNERDEAD so it can repair the shared state, instead of everyone hanging forever.

Gene Amdahl's 1967 rule for the best speed-up from parallel hardware: if a fraction s of the work must run serially, N cores give at most 1 / (s + (1 − s) / N), and never more than 1 / s however many cores you add.
example: If 10% of the work runs under one global lock, 16 cores give at most 6.4 times the speed and unlimited cores at most 10 times.

definition: How many times faster a program runs on several cores than on one: the single-core running time divided by the multi-core running time.
The share of a program's running time that can only run on one thread at a time, for example code under a single global lock. In Amdahl's law it caps the possible speed-up.

How much data each lock protects. Coarse-grained locking (one lock for a whole table) is simple but serialises everything; fine-grained locking (one lock per bucket or object) allows more parallelism, at the cost of more lock operations and more chances of deadlock.

The single global lock Linux used when SMP support arrived in version 2.0, so that only one CPU at a time ran most kernel code. It was gradually replaced by fine-grained locks and removed in Linux 2.6.39 (2011).

Splitting one data structure into several independently locked parts (stripes or segments), for example by key hash, so threads touching different parts do not contend. Early Java ConcurrentHashMap used 16 segments by default.

Java's thread-safe hash map in java.util.concurrent. Before Java 8 it used lock striping (16 segments by default); since Java 8 it uses CAS to fill an empty bin and locks only the first node of a bin that is already occupied.

A widely used object-oriented programming language that runs on the Java Virtual Machine. It has built-in threads, monitors (synchronized) and a formal memory model, revised for Java 5 (2004) by JSR-133.
One slot of a hash table's array: every key whose hash maps to that slot is stored there. Java's ConcurrentHashMap calls buckets bins.

Input/output: reading or writing disks, networks, terminals and other devices. It is slow (microseconds to milliseconds) compared with memory, so doing it while holding a hot lock makes every waiter wait too.
A tool that measures where a program spends its time, or which locks it waits on, so you optimise what actually matters.
Linux's performance-analysis tool; its perf lock command reports which kernel locks are contended and for how long.

Slowdown when threads write different variables that happen to sit in the same cache line: each write takes the whole line from the other cores, so they contend even though they share no data. Padding hot variables onto separate lines fixes it.

A high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread, while a medium-priority thread preempts the low one, so the high-priority thread is effectively blocked by unrelated medium work. It caused repeated resets on NASA's Mars Pathfinder in 1997.

The fix for priority inversion: while a thread holds a lock that a higher-priority thread is waiting for, it temporarily runs at the waiter's priority, so medium-priority threads cannot preempt it. It needs a lock with a known owner, such as a mutex.
NASA lander that reached Mars on 4 July 1997. Its software then suffered repeated system resets caused by priority inversion, fixed remotely by enabling priority inheritance on the mutex involved.
A number the scheduler uses to choose which runnable thread to run first; a higher-priority thread can preempt a lower-priority one.
One billionth of a second (0.000000001 s). One clock cycle of a 3 GHz CPU lasts about 0.33 ns.
One millionth of a second (0.000001 s), a thousand nanoseconds.
One thousandth of a second (0.001 s). Scheduler time slices are typically a few milliseconds.
Eight bits: the smallest unit of memory a CPU can address individually. A cache line is typically 64 bytes.
Describes a value, register or address that is that many binary digits wide. A 16-bit value can hold 65,536 different values, a 32-bit one about 4.3 billion and a 64-bit one about 1.8 × 10^19.
One billion bytes (1,000,000,000), in the decimal convention used here.
The POSIX error code "interrupted function call": a blocking call such as sem_wait returned early because a signal handler ran. The caller normally retries.
The POSIX error code "resource temporarily unavailable, try again". FUTEX_WAIT returns it when the futex word no longer holds the expected value.
The POSIX error code "operation not permitted". An error-checking mutex returns it when a thread unlocks a mutex it does not own.
Python's general exception for errors that fit no more specific category. The threading module raises it, for example, when a Condition is waited on without holding its lock.
Python's exception for an argument of the right type but an unacceptable value. BoundedSemaphore raises it when released more times than it was acquired.
A computer built into a device to do one job, such as a washing-machine controller, often with a single core and a small real-time operating system.
A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site instead of making a call. Once inlined, the compiler can see that the code never writes a variable and optimise accordingly.
Dutch computer scientist (1930–2002) who introduced semaphores in the 1960s, posed the dining philosophers problem and received the 1972 Turing Award.

The two semaphore operations. Wait (Dijkstra's P, also called down, acquire or sem_wait) decrements the counter, blocking while it is 0; signal (V, also up, release or sem_post) increments it and wakes one waiter if there is one.
One unit of a semaphore's counter: the right for one thread to proceed. A wait takes a permit, blocking if none is left; a signal gives one back.
example: A semaphore created with 3 permits lets three threads in at once; the fourth waits.

definition: A semaphore whose count is only ever 0 or 1. It can be used like a lock, but it has no owner, so any thread may post it.
A semaphore whose count can be any number from 0 upwards, used to limit how many threads use a set of identical resources at once.
A fixed set of identical, reusable resources, such as database connections, handed out to threads and returned after use. A counting semaphore initialised to the pool size limits how many are in use.
Python's semaphore that raises ValueError if it is released more times than it was acquired (pushing the count above its initial value), which catches double-release bugs.
Python's counting semaphore: acquire() takes a permit (or, with blocking=False, returns False instead of waiting) and release() returns one. It may be released any number of times.

The POSIX call that initialises an unnamed semaphore of type sem_t: sem_init(&s, pshared, value). A pshared of 0 means the semaphore is shared only between threads of one process; value is the initial count.

A queue where threads sleep until some condition on shared state might have become true. It is always used with a mutex: wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then re-acquires it before returning; signal or broadcast wakes waiters. Unlike a semaphore it has no memory.

The POSIX condition-variable wait: called with the mutex held, it atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and re-acquires the mutex before returning. pthread_cond_timedwait also gives up at a deadline. Either may return spuriously, so it belongs in a while loop.
Wakes at least one thread waiting on a condition variable, if any are waiting; with no waiters it does nothing and is not remembered. Python's notify() and Java's notify() play the same role.

Wakes every thread waiting on a condition variable, so each re-checks its own condition. Java's notifyAll and Python's notify_all do the same. Needed when waiters wait for different conditions, at the risk of a thundering herd.

The shared variable (a flag, a count, a queue length) that records the condition threads wait for. A condition variable is only the waiting room; the truth lives in the state variable, protected by the mutex.
A true-or-false test; here, the condition a waiting thread re-checks, such as "the queue is not empty".

The condition-variable rule used by POSIX, Java and Python: a signal only makes a waiter runnable, and it must re-acquire the mutex later, by which time another thread may have changed the state. So waiters must re-check in a while loop. Named after Xerox PARC's Mesa language (Lampson and Redell, 1980).

The original monitor rule from Tony Hoare: signal hands the mutex directly to the woken thread, so the condition it waited for is guaranteed to still hold when it runs. It gives a stronger guarantee but is rarely used by real thread libraries.
British computer scientist who invented quicksort, developed monitors (1974) and Communicating Sequential Processes, and gave the dining philosophers problem its present name. Turing Award 1980.
A return from a condition-variable wait when nobody signalled. POSIX explicitly allows it, which is one reason a wait always sits in a loop that re-checks the condition.
A thread state: ready to run and waiting only for the scheduler to give it a CPU core, as opposed to running or sleeping.
Many sleeping threads woken at once for something only one of them can use: they all contend for the mutex, and all but one go back to sleep, wasting CPU.
example: A broadcast to 100 consumers for one new item wakes 100 threads; 99 find nothing.

definition: A language construct that groups shared data with methods that run under one implicit lock, plus condition variables for waiting inside them. Devised by Per Brinch Hansen and Tony Hoare in the early 1970s; Java's synchronized objects are monitors.
Danish-American computer scientist (1938–2007) who, with Tony Hoare, developed the monitor concept and built the Concurrent Pascal language.
Java keyword that makes a method or block run while holding the object's intrinsic lock. Every Java object has one such lock and one condition, used with wait(), notify() and notifyAll().
Java exception thrown when a thread blocked in wait(), sleep() or similar is interrupted by another thread.

Java's standard concurrency library (since Java 5): thread pools, concurrent collections such as ConcurrentHashMap, atomic variables, and, in java.util.concurrent.locks, explicit locks that can have several Condition objects.
Python's condition variable: it combines a lock with wait(), notify() and notify_all(). wait_for(predicate) runs the re-check loop for you, returning once the predicate is true.
Python's double-ended queue (collections.deque), with fast appends and pops at both ends; popleft removes from the front.
Python keyword for a small anonymous function written inline, such as lambda: items, which returns the current items each time it is called.
A limit on how long an operation may wait before giving up, such as pthread_cond_timedwait returning at a deadline.

The classic problem of producers putting items into a buffer of fixed size and consumers taking them out: producers must wait when it is full, consumers when it is empty, and the buffer must never be corrupted. Also called the bounded-buffer problem.
In a producer–consumer setup, a producer is a thread that creates items and puts them into a shared buffer or queue; a consumer is a thread that takes them out and handles them.
A region of memory that holds data temporarily between the code that produces it and the code that uses it.
A fixed-size buffer used as if its end joined its start: read and write indices move forward and wrap from the last slot back to slot 0.
example: With 5 slots, the slot after 4 is (4 + 1) mod 5 = 0.

definition: The remainder after whole-number division: 7 mod 5 is 2. In C it is written %. Stepping with (i + 1) mod N runs through 0 to N − 1 and then wraps back to 0.
One step in a chain of processing steps, each passing its output to the next, usually through a queue.
The kernel queue of fully established TCP connections waiting for a server to call accept(). Its maximum length is set by listen()'s backlog argument.

A one-way kernel buffer connecting one process’s output to another’s input, as in cat log | grep error. A writer blocks when the buffer is full (by default 65,536 bytes on Linux, 16 pages of 4 KiB), which gives natural back-pressure.
The Unix command that prints the lines of its input that match a pattern.
A first-in, first-out (FIFO) collection: items are added at the back and removed from the front.

Python's thread-safe FIFO queue from the queue module, built from a lock and condition variables. With maxsize above 0, put blocks while it is full and get blocks while it is empty; maxsize 0 or less (the default) means unbounded.
A special value, such as None, put into a queue to mean "no more items", so consumers know to stop.
A queue with no size limit: put never blocks, so if producers outpace consumers it grows until memory runs out.
Slowing producers down to the pace of consumers, for example because a bounded queue makes put block when it is full, instead of letting work pile up without limit.
The classic problem of letting any number of readers use shared data at once while giving each writer exclusive access. Simple solutions starve either writers or readers.
A read-write policy where new readers may join active readers even while a writer is waiting. It maximises read throughput but can starve writers; glibc's pthread_rwlock_t uses it by default.
A read-write policy where, once a writer is waiting, newly arriving readers must wait. It prevents writer starvation but a steady stream of writers can starve readers.
When a waiting writer never gets in because readers keep overlapping, so the reader count never drops to zero.

A gate, often a semaphore initialised to 1, that every thread passes through one at a time on the way in. In a fair readers–writers solution a waiting writer holds it, so readers arriving later queue behind the writer.
First in, first out: serving requests in arrival order, like a queue at a shop counter.
A guarantee about the order in which waiting threads get a lock, usually roughly arrival order, so none waits indefinitely. Plain spinlocks and many mutexes are not fair.

A lock with two modes: shared (read) mode, which any number of readers can hold at once, and exclusive (write) mode, which one writer holds alone. In POSIX it is pthread_rwlock_t, taken with rdlock or wrlock.
Java's read-write lock in java.util.concurrent.locks. Constructed with fair set to true, it grants the lock approximately in arrival order.
The table a router or kernel consults to decide where to send each network packet, based on its destination address. It is read for every packet and rarely changed: a classic read-mostly structure.
The fixed-size block in which a database stores and caches rows on disk and in memory; 8 KB by default in PostgreSQL.

Dijkstra's 1965 problem, told as five philosophers round a table with one chopstick between each pair: each needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat. If all pick up their left chopstick at once they deadlock. It models threads needing several locks at once.

A chain of threads in which each waits for a resource held by the next, closing in a loop. It is one of the conditions needed for deadlock, so breaking it (for example by lock ordering) prevents deadlock.
Preventing deadlock by giving every lock or resource a number and always acquiring them in increasing order. Waits can then only point "upwards", so no circular wait can form.
example: Lock two bank accounts in ID order, whichever direction the transfer goes.

definition: If more items are shared out among fewer boxes, at least one box must get two or more. In the dining philosophers, five chopsticks shared among at most four diners means that not every diner can be left holding just one, so at least one diner can get two and eat.

In the dining philosophers problem, a single coordinator (the "waiter", a mutex or monitor) that hands out both chopsticks at once or neither, so nobody ever holds one chopstick while waiting for another.

K. Mani Chandy and Jayadev Misra's 1984 dining-philosophers solution: chopsticks are marked dirty or clean and passed between neighbours on request, giving a distributed solution free of deadlock and starvation.
A scheduling technique that gradually raises a waiting thread's priority the longer it waits, so it cannot starve.

A classic problem, attributed to Dijkstra (1965): a barber sleeps when there are no customers, customers wake him or sit in a limited number of waiting chairs, and leave if none is free. It models a server with a bounded waiting queue.
Deliberately rejecting new work when a system is full, like customers leaving a full barbershop, so it stays responsive instead of queuing without limit.
A fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a shared queue, avoiding the cost of creating a thread per task. A bounded queue in front of it can reject work when full.
A thread holding one resource while waiting for another. It is one of the conditions needed for deadlock.

John Little's result from queueing theory: the mean number of items in a system equals their arrival rate times the mean time each spends in it (L = λ × W). It holds for any stable system over the long run.
example: 5,000 reads per second each lasting 0.002 s means about 10 reads in progress at once on average.

definition: Publishing a new version of a data structure by atomically replacing the one pointer readers follow, so each reader sees either the whole old version or the whole new one, never a mix.
Never changed after it is created. An immutable object can be shared between threads without locking, as long as it is published safely and its memory is not reclaimed too early.
Freeing memory that concurrent readers might still be using, only once no thread can still reach it. Lock-free structures need a scheme for this: garbage collection, hazard pointers, epochs or RCU.
The period between an object's creation and its destruction, during which it is valid to access. Concurrent code must make sure no thread uses an object after another has freed it.

In thread synchronisation, the operation that wakes a waiting thread: posting a semaphore (sem_post, V) or signalling a condition variable (pthread_cond_signal). A semaphore remembers a signal in its count; a condition variable forgets one sent when nobody is waiting. Separately, a Unix signal is an asynchronous notification the kernel delivers to a process, such as SIGINT, which can interrupt a blocking wait.

The rules for when, and in what order, one thread's memory writes become visible to other threads. Compilers and CPUs reorder accesses for speed, so code must use atomics, locks or fences to get the ordering it needs.
American computer scientist who defined sequential consistency (1979) and invented logical clocks and the Paxos algorithm. Turing Award 2013.
The C11 header that provides atomic types, the atomic_load, atomic_store, atomic_fetch_add and atomic_compare_exchange functions, and the memory_order constants.

A compiler or CPU making memory accesses take effect in a different order from program order. It is invisible to the thread itself but visible to other threads, which is why shared data needs atomics or locks.

A compiler optimisation that moves an operation out of a loop because it believes the result cannot change inside it, for example loading a flag once instead of on every iteration. It is legal because data races are assumed never to happen.
Device registers that appear at memory addresses, so reading or writing those addresses talks to the hardware. This, not threading, is what C's volatile is for.

A CPU technique of executing later instructions while earlier ones wait (for example on memory). The thread still sees program-order results, but other cores can observe its memory accesses in a different order.
Describes a memory model, such as ARM's or POWER's, that may reorder almost any memory accesses unless code asks otherwise with barriers or acquire/release instructions.
IBM's processor architecture, used in its servers. Like ARM it is weakly ordered.
The US computing company. R. Kent Treiber published his lock-free stack in an IBM research report in 1986, and IBM designs the POWER processors.
A tiny multi-threaded program with a specific outcome, used to probe what a memory model allows, such as the store-buffering and message-passing tests.

The pattern where one thread writes data and then sets a flag, while another waits for the flag and then reads the data. It is correct only if the flag store is a release and the flag load an acquire (or stronger).

An instruction or function call (a fence) that stops memory accesses being reordered across it, without being attached to a particular variable. C11 provides atomic_thread_fence; x86 has mfence and ARM dmb.
x86's full memory fence: every load and store before it completes before any after it, which drains the store buffer.
ARM's data memory barrier instruction; with the ish option it orders memory accesses as seen by all cores in the inner shareable domain (in practice, every core).

An ordering on a store: no memory access before it (in program order) may be moved after it. Everything the thread wrote earlier is published along with it, to any thread that reads the value with acquire semantics.

An ordering on a load: no memory access after it (in program order) may be moved before it. If it reads a value written by a release store, everything before that release is visible after the acquire.
The C11 memory order for read-modify-write operations that act as both an acquire and a release, such as a CAS that takes a lock and also publishes data.
The weakest C11 memory order: the operation is still atomic, so no update is lost, but it orders nothing else. Fine for statistics counters, wrong for publishing data.

C11's strongest and default memory order: all seq_cst operations appear in one total order that every thread agrees on, on top of acquire/release guarantees. On x86 a seq_cst store compiles to xchg (or mov plus mfence).
A C11 memory order meant to order only accesses that depend on the loaded value. Compilers implement it as acquire, and its use is discouraged.

The memory-model link between threads: a release store and an acquire load that reads its value, an unlock and a later lock of the same mutex, thread creation and the new thread's start, or a thread's end and the join that waits for it.
The memory-model ordering of operations within one thread: one operation is sequenced-before another if it comes earlier in that thread's program order.
The property that orderings chain: if A is before B and B is before C, then A is before C. Happens-before is transitive, which is how a release/acquire pair orders data written before the release.
ARMv8's load-acquire (ldar) and store-release (stlr) instructions, which C11 acquire loads and release stores compile to on ARM.
x86's basic instruction for copying between registers and memory. Because of TSO, a plain mov load already behaves as an acquire and a plain mov store as a release at the hardware level.
A statement, such as GCC's asm volatile("" ::: "memory"), that stops the compiler moving memory accesses across it but emits no CPU instruction, so the hardware can still reorder.

Linux kernel memory-barrier macros: smp_mb is a full barrier, smp_wmb orders stores, smp_rmb orders loads, and smp_store_release and smp_load_acquire give release and acquire semantics. They are documented in memory-barriers.txt.
The formal model of which orderings the Linux kernel's own atomics and barriers guarantee. Kernel code such as seqlocks follows it rather than the C11 model.
A systems programming language whose ownership rules reject data races in safe code at compile time. Its atomics use the C++ memory model.
Google's programming language with built-in lightweight threads (goroutines) and channels. It has its own happens-before memory model.
Java Specification Request 133, which rewrote the Java memory model for Java 5 (2004). It gave volatile acquire/release semantics, which made double-checked locking with a volatile field correct.

Lazy initialisation that checks the pointer without a lock, then takes the lock and checks again. Without acquire/release atomics it is broken: another thread can see the pointer before the object's fields.
An object of which a program creates exactly one shared instance, often lazily on first use.
In C, the special pointer value meaning "points to nothing". Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour and usually crashes.
The C++11 guarantee that a function-local static variable is initialised exactly once, even if several threads call the function at the same time; other callers wait until it is done.
The POSIX call that runs an initialisation function exactly once, however many threads call it; the others wait until it has finished.
A Python decorator (since 3.9) that remembers a function's results by argument. It does not promise the function body runs only once if several threads call it at the same time.
C's standard function for allocating heap memory; free gives it back. A freed block may be handed out again at the same address by the next malloc.
A CPU running instructions before it knows they are needed, for example loading data early, and discarding the work if it guessed wrong. An early load can return an old value if nothing orders it.
An ordering in which every pair of items is ranked one before the other. All seq_cst operations fall into one total order that every thread agrees on.
Computer scientist at the University of Maryland who led the revision of the Java memory model (JSR-133) and organised the "Double-Checked Locking is Broken" declaration.
The instructions a CPU actually executes; assembly language is its human-readable text form, such as mov eax, [counter].
C's standard function for printing formatted text, such as printf("%d", data).
A C type that groups several named fields into one object, such as a node with a value and a next pointer.
A promise about what happens when threads are delayed: blocking (a stalled thread can stop everyone), obstruction-free, lock-free or wait-free, from weakest to strongest.

A progress guarantee: however threads are delayed, some thread always completes its operation in a finite number of steps. A stalled thread cannot stop the others, though an individual thread may starve.
The strongest progress guarantee: every thread completes each operation in a bounded number of its own steps, however the others behave.
A weak progress guarantee: a thread finishes in a bounded number of steps if every other thread pauses. Contending threads may keep undoing each other's work.
An algorithm in which one stalled thread can prevent others from completing, as with any mutex or spinlock whose holder is suspended.
A function the OS runs in a thread when a Unix signal (such as SIGINT from Ctrl-C) arrives, interrupting whatever the thread was doing.

Computer scientist whose 1991 paper "Wait-free synchronization" showed that atomic primitives differ in power: loads, stores and test-and-set cannot build every wait-free structure for any number of threads, while compare-and-swap can.
The basic lock-free pattern: read the current value, compute a new one privately, then compare-and-swap it in; if the CAS fails because another thread changed the value first, start again.

R. Kent Treiber's 1986 lock-free stack: a linked list whose top pointer is updated with compare-and-swap. In languages without garbage collection it suffers from the ABA problem and needs safe memory reclamation.
A collection where the last item added is the first one removed (last in, first out): push adds an item on top and pop takes the top item off. Not to be confused with a thread’s call stack.
example: Push A, then B, then C: the next pop returns C.

definition: The two operations of a stack (last in, first out): push puts an item on top, pop removes and returns the top item.

A failure of compare-and-swap: a value changes from A to something else and back to A, so the CAS succeeds although the structure underneath has changed. In a lock-free stack it can link in freed nodes.
example: Top goes A, B, C, then A again (a reused node); a stalled thread's CAS from A succeeds with a stale next pointer.

definition: A pointer paired with a version counter, compared and swapped together; every successful update increments the counter, so a pointer that has come back no longer matches. It fixes ABA as long as the counter cannot wrap round to the same value meanwhile.
Reading or writing memory after it has been freed. The memory may have been reused or returned to the OS, so the program may crash or silently read garbage.

Maged Michael's 2004 reclamation scheme: before dereferencing a node, a thread publishes its address in a per-thread hazard slot; a thread wanting to free a node first checks every slot and defers the free if the node is listed.

A reclamation scheme in which threads announce the global epoch they are active in, and retired nodes are freed once every active thread has moved past the epoch in which they were retired. Cheap per access, but one stalled thread can halt all freeing.
A Rust library of concurrency tools, including crossbeam-epoch for epoch-based reclamation and lock-free queues.
Maged Michael and Michael Scott's 1996 lock-free FIFO queue, which uses compare-and-swap on both the head and the tail pointers. Java's ConcurrentLinkedQueue is based on it.
Java's unbounded thread-safe queue in java.util.concurrent, based on the Michael–Scott lock-free queue.
The ISO working group (ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG21) that writes the C++ standard. Its proposals are numbered papers such as P2530.

The WG21 paper “Hazard pointers for C++26”, which adds hazard pointers to the C++ standard library (the <hazard_pointer> header). It was voted into the C++26 working draft in June 2023; check that your standard library actually ships it before relying on it.

The WG21 paper that adds read-copy-update (RCU) to the C++ standard library (the <rcu> header). It was voted into the C++26 working draft in June 2023; check that your standard library actually ships it before relying on it.
A part of the Domain Name System namespace managed as one unit, such as example.com and its subdomains, served from one set of records.
The counter inside a read-write lock recording how many readers hold it. Every reader entering or leaving updates it atomically, so its cache line can become a bottleneck.
Two readers holding a read-write lock each try to upgrade to write mode; each waits for the other to stop reading, so neither ever can.

A reader-writer mechanism in which the writer increments a sequence counter before and after each update (odd means a write is in progress), and readers copy the data, then retry if the counter was odd or changed. Readers write nothing shared.
A read that combines parts of two different writes, such as the high half of an old 64-bit value with the low half of a new one, because it ran in the middle of an update.
The kernel's tracking of the current time, updated on timer ticks and read very often by programs.
The POSIX call that returns the current time of a given clock. On Linux it is usually served without entering the kernel, by reading seqlock-protected timekeeping data.

The periodic interrupt from a hardware timer that drives timekeeping and scheduling. On Linux its rate is the kernel’s HZ setting, chosen when the kernel is configured: 100, 250, 300 or 1,000 times a second.
A number recording a moment in time, often a count of timer ticks or nanoseconds since some starting point.
Base-16 notation using the digits 0–9 and A–F, written with a 0x prefix in C; each hex digit stands for 4 bits, so 0xFFFFFFFF is the largest 32-bit value.

Read-copy-update: a technique in which writers copy data, modify the copy, publish it with one pointer store, then free the old version only after a grace period. Readers take no locks and write nothing shared. Used throughout the Linux kernel since 2002.
In RCU, the wait until every reader that might still hold the old version has left its read-side critical section. Only after it can the old version be freed.
Linux kernel developer who co-invented RCU and has long maintained the kernel's RCU implementation.
The Linux kernel's in-memory cache of file-path lookups (directory entries), read on almost every file access and protected largely by RCU.
The code between rcu_read_lock() and rcu_read_unlock() in which a reader may use RCU-protected data. A grace period waits for every such section that began before it.
The RCU call a writer uses to publish a new version: a pointer store with release semantics, so readers that see the new pointer also see the fully built object.
The RCU call a reader uses to load an RCU-protected pointer with the ordering needed to read the object it points to safely.
The RCU call that blocks until a grace period has passed: every read-side critical section that began before the call has finished.
The RCU call that registers a callback, such as one freeing the old version, to run after a grace period, so the writer does not have to block.
A function handed to other code to be called later, when some event happens.
A library that provides RCU to ordinary (user-space) programs, with several flavours that differ in how readers are tracked.
Making a newly built object visible to other threads, typically by storing a pointer to it with release semantics, so that any thread that sees the pointer also sees the object's complete contents.

Changing shared data by building a modified private copy and then switching readers over to it with one pointer swap, instead of modifying the data in place; readers already holding the old version keep using it unchanged. RCU and Java’s CopyOnWriteArrayList work this way; operating systems use the same idea for memory pages after fork().
Java's thread-safe list in which every write copies the whole underlying array, so reads need no locking; it suits lists that are read far more often than written.
Data that was correct a moment ago but has since been replaced; RCU readers may briefly see it after an update.
Meta's open-source C++ library, which includes hazard pointers and other concurrent data structures.
The Boost C++ library's collection of lock-free queues and stacks.
The crash when a program touches memory it may not access, such as an unmapped page; the kernel sends it the SIGSEGV signal.
Remove a range of pages from a process's address space (munmap on Linux). Any later access to it causes a segmentation fault.
The fixed-size block, usually 4 KiB, in which the OS manages virtual memory and maps it to physical memory.
The library code behind malloc and free that hands out and recycles heap memory. It readily reuses a freed block's address for a later allocation.
A variable holding the memory address of something else. Following it to reach the target is called dereferencing.
Following a pointer to read or write the thing it points at, as in old->next. Dereferencing a pointer to freed memory is a use-after-free.
One element of a linked structure, holding a value and a pointer to the next element.
